section.title: Laborers in the Vineyard
section.sectionRationale: The parable of the vineyard workers illustrates the reversal Jesus just spoke, the last will be first, exposing the grumbling heart that resents grace. Then, a third time, Jesus foretells His death, corrects a grasp for status with the definition of greatness as service, and heals two blind men who see and follow.
section.thesis: God's kingdom runs on His sovereign generosity, not on human merit or seniority, so the grasping heart must be undone; greatness is service, and the Son of Man Himself comes not to be served but to give His life as a ransom for many.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the parable of the workers and the generous landowner; the third passion prediction; the request for thrones answered by the call to servanthood and the ransom saying; and the healing of two blind men outside Jericho.

verses.text: “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day and sent them into his vineyard.
About the third hour he went out and saw others standing in the marketplace doing nothing.
‘You also go into my vineyard,’ he said, ‘and I will pay you whatever is right.’
So they went. He went out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour and did the same thing.
About the eleventh hour he went out and found still others standing around. ‘Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?’ he asked.
‘Because no one has hired us,’ they answered. So he told them, ‘You also go into my vineyard.’
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first.’
The workers who were hired about the eleventh hour came and each received a denarius.
So when the original workers came, they assumed they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
On receiving their pay, they began to grumble against the landowner.
‘These men who were hired last worked only one hour,’ they said, ‘and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.’
But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius?
Take your pay and go. I want to give this last man the same as I gave you.
Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’
So the last will be first, and the first will be last.”

units.label: The passion foretold a third time

verses.text: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside and said,
“Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death
and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life.”

units.label: Greatness is service
units.note: the Son of Man came to give His life

verses.text: Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to Jesus with her sons and knelt down to make a request of Him.
“What do you want?” He inquired. She answered, “Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left.”
“You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?” “We can,” the brothers answered.
“You will indeed drink My cup,” Jesus said. “But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them.”
When the ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers.
But Jesus called them aside and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them.
It shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your {{diakonos|servant}},
and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave,
just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a {{lytron|ransom}} for many.”
As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed Him.
And there were two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!”
The crowd admonished them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!”
Jesus stopped and called them. “What do you want Me to do for you?” He asked.
“Lord,” they answered, “let our eyes be opened.”
Moved with {{splanchnizomai|compassion}}, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him.

diakonos.gloss: A servant, one who waits on others, the root of the word deacon. Jesus overturns worldly greatness: in His kingdom the great one is the servant, and the first is the slave, on the pattern of the serving Son of Man.

lytron.gloss: A ransom, the price paid to release a captive or slave. The Son of Man gives His life as a ransom in the place of many, the heart of the gospel: His death purchases the freedom of those held by sin and death.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion from the depths. It is Jesus' gut-level mercy for the two blind men whom the crowd would silence, the same compassion that runs through His whole ministry.

basic.context: Jesus tells of a landowner who hires workers through the day and pays them all the same wage, from the first at dawn to the last at the eleventh hour. The all-day workers grumble; the owner answers that he has been just to them and is free to be generous. Jesus foretells His death a third time, in fuller detail. When James and John's mother asks for the top thrones, Jesus redefines greatness as service and reveals He came to give His life as a ransom. Then He heals two blind beggars who call Him Son of David.
basic.hermeneutics: The parable illustrates the saying that brackets it, the last will be first. It is not about labor economics but about grace: God gives the kingdom freely, and the merit-minded resent it. Notice the contrast: right after Jesus foretells His self-giving death, the disciples grasp for status, and He corrects them with His own example, the ransom.
basic.originalLanguages: Greatness in the kingdom belongs to the diakonos, the servant. The Son of Man gives His life as a lytron, a ransom, in the place of many. And He heals the blind men because He is moved with splanchnizomai, compassion from the depths.
basic.typology: The vineyard is a familiar image of God's people. The cup Jesus will drink is the cup of God's judgment the prophets spoke of. The ransom fulfills the servant of Isaiah 53 who pours out His life for many.
basic.christ: Jesus is the generous landowner's Lord, the Son of Man who will be mocked, flogged, and crucified, and the Servant who gives His life as a ransom for many. He is the Son of David whose compassion opens blind eyes and draws the healed to follow Him.
basic.god: God is free and generous, giving grace as He pleases and refusing to let human bookkeeping bind Him. He is just to all and lavish beyond desert, and He prepares places in His kingdom according to His own will.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 foretells the servant who pours out His life for many. Isaiah 5 pictures God's vineyard. Philippians 2 shows Christ taking the form of a servant. Mark 10 parallels the ransom saying and the blind man of Jericho.
basic.oneStory: As Jesus climbs toward Jerusalem, He unmasks the grasping heart that resents grace and craves status, and He sets against it His own path: the Son of Man who serves and gives His life as a ransom for many. The kingdom comes by His self-giving, not our merit, and the last are made first. The blind who cry for mercy see and follow, a picture of all who receive the ransom by faith.

context.literary:
The chapter begins with a conjunction that English hides. Matthew 20:1 opens with for, and it ties the parable to the saying that closed chapter 19, that many who are first will be last and the last first. The parable then ends with the saying turned round, the last will be first and the first will be last, verse 16. Everything between is a single story built to illustrate that frame, and the frame also encloses Peter's question about what the disciples will get, 19:27. The parable is a reply to a man who asked for a reckoning.

The parable itself is built in two panels. The first panel, verses 1 to 7, is a series of five hirings: a bargain at dawn, a promise of whatever is right at the third, sixth and ninth hours, and at the eleventh hour no terms at all. The second panel, verses 8 to 15, is the reckoning, in which the order of payment is reversed so that the early workers can see what the late ones receive. The later workers are given no figure, only the owner's word in verse 4, so that the reader, like the workers, has to trust him.

After the parable the chapter moves in a rising line. The third announcement of the passion in verses 17 to 19 is the most detailed of the three, and it is followed at once by a request for status from the sons of Zebedee, verses 20 to 28, which shows that the lesson of the first panel is not yet learned. The final scene, verses 29 to 34, is the counterweight. The two blind men ask for mercy and ask for sight, and Jesus asks them exactly the question He asked the mother of James and John, What do you want Me to do for you, verse 32 against verse 21. One request is for thrones and the other for eyes. The passage ends with the healed men following Jesus, which is the only verb of discipleship in the chapter that is actually carried out.
context.historical:
A day labourer in the first century stood in the marketplace and waited to be hired, and a denarius was customarily a day's wage, as the BSB footnote to verse 2 says. The workers who are still waiting at the eleventh hour, about five in the afternoon, are not lazy. They say no one has hired us, verse 7. In the world of subsistence labour a man who was not hired did not eat that evening, and a landowner who hired late was, in effect, feeding a family. The grumbling of the early workers has to be heard against that background: they were paid the agreed wage, and what they resent is that others were paid for need.

The vineyard belongs to Israel's imagery. Isaiah 5:1-7 sings of a vineyard on a fertile hill that yielded sour fruit, and Isaiah 27:2-6 sings of the day when the vineyard is fruitful and fills the world. Jeremiah 12:10 laments that many shepherds destroyed it. Anyone who heard a parable about a landowner and his vineyard would at once think of God and his people.

The third announcement of the passion is given on the road, as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, verse 17. Jerusalem lies on a ridge, and the pilgrim road up from Jericho was a steep climb of roughly fifteen miles. Jericho was the last stop before that climb, and pilgrims for the feasts passed through it in crowds, which is why the beggars sat by the road. The announcement names the Gentiles for the first time as those who will mock, flog and crucify, and crucifixion was a Roman penalty, a death that Jewish hearers knew as the most shameful.

The cup was a familiar image of God's judgment. Psalm 75:8 speaks of a cup of foaming wine in the LORD's hand, Isaiah 51:17 of the cup of His fury drained to the dregs, and Jeremiah 25:15 of the cup of the wine of wrath. The mother of the sons of Zebedee kneeling with her request was following the custom of petitioning a ruler, and the mother is also found at the cross, Matthew 27:56.
context.canonical:
The parable's vineyard sits in a long line of vineyard texts, from Isaiah 5 to Jesus' own parable of the tenants in Matthew 21:33-41. In Isaiah the owner expects sweet grapes and finds sour fruit, and in Matthew 21 the tenants refuse to give him his share. In Matthew 20 the opposite problem arises, a vineyard in which the owner is generous and the workers complain. The three texts together show a God who gives, and people who either resist the giving or resent it. Jonah 4:1-2 supplies a close parallel in a man who is angry because God is gracious and compassionate, and Luke 15:28-30 gives the elder brother who refuses to join the feast because his father has been generous.

The ransom saying of verse 28 is the fullest statement in Matthew of what the cross achieves, and it stands on the shoulders of Isaiah 53. There the Servant makes His life a guilt offering, justifies many and bears their iniquities, Isaiah 53:10-12. Mark records the same saying in Mark 10:45, and Paul states it in 1 Timothy 2:5-6, who gave Himself as a ransom for all, and Titus 2:14, who gave Himself for us to redeem us. Peter says the redeeming price was the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The older background lies in the law, where a man could redeem his life by paying a ransom, Exodus 21:30, and a kinsman could redeem a relative who had sold himself, Leviticus 25:48-49.

The healing of the blind belongs to the signs of the age to come in Isaiah 35:5 and Isaiah 42:7. The title Son of David, which the blind men use twice, has appeared on the lips of two blind men in Matthew 9:27 and the Canaanite woman in Matthew 15:22, and it is shouted by the crowd at Jerusalem in Matthew 21:9. Matthew uses it as the title of the King whose coming means mercy.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew gives this parable to correct a reasoning that his own church would have found natural, that service ought to be paid by length and that a late arrival ought to stand behind those who came early. Peter's question in 19:27, we have left everything, what then will there be for us, is a fair question, and the parable answers it in a way that is both reassuring and unsettling. The reassurance is that the kingdom's reward is not meagre, for each receives a full day's pay. The unsettling element is that the reward is given by the owner's goodness, not by the worker's record, so that no one in the vineyard can use his labour as a lever.

The ending of the chapter belongs with the parable in Matthew's mind. A parable about grace is followed by two events, a request for status and a request for sight, and between them stands the most explicit statement of the cross in the Gospel so far. The disciples need to be shown that grace does not leave pride standing, and that the way to greatness is a path of service marked out by the Son of Man.

Matthew also has an eye on the church's later struggles. Jewish believers who had borne the heat of the day found Gentiles admitted on equal terms, and whatever the original setting, the parable gives a way to hold that tension, with an owner who is not unfair to anyone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
A parable describes how the kingdom works, and it is not a lesson in labour relations or a guide to how employers should pay. Reading it as wage policy misses the point. The landowner's right to do as he pleases with what is his, verse 15, is a statement about God and not about anyone's boss.

The prescriptive force is in the final saying and the three conversations that follow. Jesus says directly, It shall not be this way among you, verse 26, about the Gentile model of rulers who lord it over others. The way of greatness is service, and this is stated as a command to the whole community. The cup is described, not prescribed: Jesus says that James and John will drink it, and the church later sees what that meant for each of them.

The gift of sight is a record of what happened. It is not a promise that every prayer for healing will be answered in the same way. What does carry over is the pattern: the blind men cry out, will not be silenced, and are heard by a Lord who stops, calls and asks what they want.

debates.question: Who are the workers who come early and late?

views.label: Jews and Gentiles
views.case: The workers hired at dawn are Israel, who bore the burden of the law, and the later workers are the Gentiles who come in at the last hour. The grumbling is the resentment of those who had every privilege at the welcome of outsiders. This was a common reading in the early church.

views.label: Lifelong disciples and late converts
views.case: The parable is about the people of God in every age, and the point is that someone converted on a deathbed receives the same salvation as one who served for decades. Luke 23:42-43 gives a picture of the same grace.

views.label: A warning to the self-righteous
views.case: The focus is not on a particular group but on the attitude of those who think that they have earned more. The parable is addressed to Peter, who asked what he would get, and to every disciple who counts.

debates.bearing: The readings are compatible, because the parable has one point. The kingdom is a gift in which the owner is good and the grumbler's problem is envy, and the same point can be applied to Jew and Gentile, to long and short service, and to every heart that counts.

debates.question: What does it mean that the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many?

views.label: A substitution that pays the price of sin
views.case: The Greek preposition anti, in the place of, together with the Servant of Isaiah 53 who bears the iniquities of many, suggests that Christ stands where sinners stand. 1 Timothy 2:6 uses a related compound word, and Romans 3:24 speaks of redemption in Christ Jesus.

views.label: A liberation from enemy powers
views.case: Others stress that a ransom is a price of release from captivity, so that the cross frees people from sin, death and the devil, as Hebrews 2:14-15 says.

views.label: A costly act of self-giving that cannot be pressed into one image
views.case: Some stress that Jesus does not say to whom the ransom is paid and that the point of the saying is the cost and the direction, a life given for others, and not a transaction.

debates.bearing: The New Testament uses all of these pictures, and they do not need to compete. At least it is clear that the many are those whom Christ releases, that the price is His own life, and that the cost fell on Him and not on them.

debates.question: Were there one or two blind men?

views.label: Matthew records two and Mark one
views.case: Mark 10:46 names one man, Bartimaeus, and Luke 18:35 has one blind man at the approach to Jericho. Matthew has two here and two in Matthew 9:27. On this view Mark and Luke tell of the more prominent man and Matthew counts both, since mentioning one does not deny the other.

views.label: A difference in tradition that is left unresolved
views.case: Some interpreters hold that the Gospels shaped a common event differently for their own purposes, and that the exact number and the place, leaving or approaching Jericho, do not carry the point.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the story depends on the number. The Gospel's point is the cry for mercy, the refusal to be silenced, the question and the answer, and the following that completes the scene.

study.originalLanguages:
The parable's pay and its protest turn on a handful of words. In verse 2 the owner agrees to pay a denarius, and the verb is symphoneo, to sound together, the origin of symphony. The workers have a contract. Verse 13 repeats the same verb when the owner reminds the grumbler, Did you not agree with me. For the later workers there is no such bargain. He says I will pay you whatever is right, dikaion, a word of justice, and they go on trust. The owner's justice is both the fairness of the contract and the generosity beyond it.

The owner's reply in verse 15 ends with the words, Or is your eye evil because I am good. The Greek is literal, ophthalmos poneros, and it is an idiom for envy or stinginess and the word for good, agathos, is the same word Jesus used in Matthew 19:17 when He said that there is only One who is good. The vineyard owner's goodness is the goodness of God, and the envious eye is the very opposite. The address friend in verse 13 is the Greek hetaire, a word Jesus uses again to Judas in Matthew 26:50, a polite word that carries distance. The workers speak of the burden and the scorching heat, in Greek the kauson, a word that can mean a burning wind, which shows how real the day's labour was. The BSB footnote to verse 16 says some manuscripts add that many are called but few are chosen, a saying that Matthew uses in Matthew 22:14.

The third passion announcement uses three verbs that are new to the sequence: they will mock, empaizo, flog, mastigoo, and crucify, stauroo. It is the first time in Jesus' predictions that crucifixion is named. The verb deliver, paradidomi, is the same verb used in 17:22, and it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses of the Servant in Isaiah 53:12.

In verse 22 Jesus asks about the cup, poterion, which in the prophets is the cup of judgment. The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add a reference to baptism, a phrase found in Mark 10:38. The word for the seats, at the right and the left, is the same pair that appears on the cross in Matthew 27:38.

In verses 26 and 27 Jesus uses two nouns that rise in strength, diakonos, one who serves, and doulos, a slave. The verb for the Gentile rulers lording it over is katakyrieuo, a compound of rule that means to dominate. Verse 28 uses lytron, ransom, a word for the price paid to free a captive or a slave. In the New Testament it occurs here and in the parallel in Mark 10:45, and its compound antilytron is found in 1 Timothy 2:6. The preposition anti, translated for, means in the place of, and many, polloi, echoes the many of Isaiah 53:11-12.

In the last scene the crowd rebukes the blind men with epitimao, the verb Jesus uses for rebuking demons, and they cry the louder. Jesus stops, and the word for compassion in verse 34, splanchnistheis, from splanchna, the inner organs, is the same verb Matthew used of the king's mercy in 18:27. The ending says that they followed Him, ekolouthesan, the same verb used of the disciples who left their nets, Matthew 4:20, and the one the rich man in 19:21 could not carry out.

typology.type: The vineyard of the LORD, Isaiah 5:1-7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's song describes God planting, clearing and guarding His vineyard, Israel, and expecting good fruit. Jesus' parable returns to the vineyard, but now the owner is out in the marketplace, seeking workers to bring into it. The vineyard is the place of God's work in the world and of His generosity. The escalation is that the owner does not merely inspect the vineyard but goes out repeatedly to bring in the idle, as Christ seeks the lost. The type falls short because Isaiah's vineyard was judged for its fruit, and Jesus' parable ends with a gift to all who came, resting on the owner's goodness and not on the yield.

typology.type: The cup of God's judgment, Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17
typology.fulfillment: The prophets describe a cup in the LORD's hand which the wicked must drink to the dregs, and Isaiah 51:17 says Jerusalem herself has drunk it. When Jesus asks can you drink the cup I am going to drink, He takes up this image for His own coming death. In Gethsemane He prays that the cup would pass from Him and yet He submits, Matthew 26:39, and on the cross He bears what the cup contains. The pattern holds, since the cup is judgment, and it is escalated in that the Son drinks it in the place of others. It falls short in that believers drink His cup only in the sense of sharing His suffering, Colossians 1:24, not in bearing wrath.

typology.type: The Servant who gives His life for many, Isaiah 53:10-12
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant makes His life a guilt offering, bears the iniquities of many and pours out His life unto death. Jesus' saying about the Son of Man picks up the same many, the same giving of life and the same service. Where Isaiah left the Servant unnamed, Jesus claims the role for Himself. Philippians 2:7 says He took the form of a servant, and Acts 8:32-35 shows the early church reading Isaiah 53 as the account of Jesus. The type falls short only in the sense that Isaiah did not say how the Servant would be exalted, and the resurrection answers that.

typology.type: The Davidic King who opens blind eyes, Isaiah 35:5 and Isaiah 42:7
typology.fulfillment: The prophets promised that in the age of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened, and that the Servant would open them. The blind men call Jesus Son of David, and He opens their eyes as the King of the promised age. John 9 shows the same sign in a man born blind. The correspondence is that the miracle is a sign of who Jesus is and not only of His kindness. The type falls short in that the healing of the eyes is a foretaste, and the full removal of blindness, and of every other loss, awaits the new creation of Revelation 21:4.

study.christ:
The parable leads first to the owner, and it is Jesus who stands behind the owner's voice. The parable does not need to be turned into a one to one code in which the owner is Christ. But the shape is plain: the One who goes out at every hour of the day and finds the idle is the One who says come to Me, all you who are weary, Matthew 11:28. His call is the call of the landowner, and the reckoning at evening is the reckoning of the One who will sit as judge and who will say friend to those who resent His goodness.

The central claim of the chapter is in the third announcement and in verse 28. Jesus goes up to Jerusalem knowing exactly what will happen: delivered to the chief priests and scribes, condemned, handed to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged and crucified, and raised on the third day. He does not drift into the cross. He names each step. Then, when the disciples' hunger for status shows, He sets His own purpose beside theirs: the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. This is the Servant of Isaiah 53 in His own words. The ransom saying does not describe an accident. It tells the reason for the incarnation.

Jesus also makes the cup His own. He tells James and John that they will drink it, but He alone drinks it as judgment, and Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39, shows how much it cost Him. The irony of verse 21 is completed on Calvary, where two men are crucified on His right and on His left, Matthew 27:38. The places the brothers wanted were taken by the robbers, and the throne of Jesus' glory was a cross. The only way to His right hand in glory is by His cup.

He is the Son of David who stops for the cry of the blind. The two men ask for mercy, and the crowd tries to silence them, and Jesus stops. The King on His way to the cross, going up to be handed over, halts for two beggars. His question, What do you want Me to do for you, is the same to the grasping mother and to the blind men, and only the second answer is a request He can grant, for what is asked is sight. He touches their eyes, and they follow Him on the road to Jerusalem, which is where the Servant will give His life.

Care is needed not to over-read the parable, since the hours of the day are not a calendar of salvation history and the denarius is not a code. The christological weight is on His goodness, His self-giving and His mercy.
study.god:
The vineyard owner shows what kind of giver God is. He is not outwitted, he is not a debtor, and he is not bound by anything but his own character. He keeps every promise he makes, paying the first workers exactly what they agreed. But he is also free to give what he wishes to those he has hired on trust. Paul asks the same question of God, who has first given to Him that He should repay, Romans 11:35, and says in Romans 9:15-16 that it does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy. The doctrine is that God owes nothing, and gives everything.

The parable also shows God as one who goes out. The owner returns to the marketplace again and again, at the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours. The picture is of an initiative that does not wait to be asked. Isaiah 55:1 calls everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters, and the hiring of the idle matches that welcome. In God's economy it is the idle who are looked for.

The text holds together two things people find hard to put together, perfect justice and extravagant generosity. The first workers are not wronged. The last are not rewarded for their merit. Both truths come from the same character. God's justice is not harmed by His mercy, and His mercy does not abolish His justice. Exodus 33:19 puts both in one verse, when God says that He will cause all His goodness to pass before Moses, and that He will have mercy on whom He will have mercy.

There is a tension in the chapter between sovereignty and love. The Father has prepared the places at the Son's right and left, verse 23, and the Son does not grant them as a favour. God has His own plan for the kingdom, and it is not subject to a mother's request, however loving. Yet the same God has compassion on two blind beggars. The sovereign who reserves the thrones is the God who stops on the road.

For worship the chapter asks for gratitude and for suspicion of the comparing heart. We worship a God who calls us when we had nothing to offer, and who pays more than a wage. We are asked to rejoice with those who come late, to give up counting, and to take the lowest place as the Son of Man did. Worship in this chapter is the response of those who have been hired from the marketplace and given the owner's own goodness.

crossReferences.note: The song of the vineyard, in which God plants Israel and looks for sweet fruit. Jesus' parable draws on the same image, and a hearer would take the landowner to represent God, with the workers the people he has called into his work.

Jonah is angry because God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. His complaint is that of the early workers, who cannot bear that the owner's goodness reaches those they thought undeserving.

The older brother refuses to join the feast because his father has been generous to a returning son. It is the same resentment as in the vineyard, spoken in a different story, and it shows how deeply the question runs in Jesus' teaching.

Paul quotes God's words to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and concludes that it does not depend on man's desire or effort but on God's mercy. It is the doctrine that the vineyard owner acts out in the right to do as he pleases with what is his.

A cup in the LORD's hand which the wicked drink down to the dregs. It supplies the background for Jesus' question to James and John, since the cup in the prophets is the cup of God's judgment, which He is about to drink Himself.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays, let this cup pass from Me, yet not as I will but as You will. The cup He asked James and John about in 20:22 is the cup He faces here, and it shows that His own willingness to drink it is costly obedience, not calm.
Two robbers are crucified, one on His right and one on His left. The seats the mother of Zebedee's sons asked for are filled in a way no one expected, and the place of glory is revealed as a cross.

The Servant makes His life a guilt offering, justifies many and bears their iniquities, and pours out His life unto death. The ransom saying in Matthew 20:28 draws its language of the many and of self-giving from this passage.

A man could redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded. It shows what a ransom meant in Israel's law, a payment that releases a life, and gives a background for the word Jesus uses of His own death.

Paul tells of Christ who emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross. It is the apostolic echo of Jesus' saying that the Son of Man came to serve, and it shows the pattern He gave for the church.

Mark's version of the request of James and John, with the sons themselves asking and the question about baptism added. Reading it with Matthew shows that the lesson on service and the ransom saying were firmly held in the tradition.
In the day of the LORD the eyes of the blind will be opened. The healing of the two men at Jericho is a sign that the day has begun, and it explains why they call out to the Son of David.

Two other blind men followed Jesus crying Have mercy on us, Son of David, and were healed. The repetition in chapter 20 gives a second round of the same cry, and shows Matthew's interest in the title and in the faith that persists.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who gives without being asked. He plants a garden, sets people in it and tells them they may eat freely. The fall turns that gift into a grievance, and the serpent's lie is that God is holding something back. The resentment of the early workers in the vineyard is the same suspicion in an older form, that God's generosity to someone else is a loss to me. The question that runs through the whole of Scripture is whether people will trust that the Giver is good.

The story of Israel's vineyard is the story of a God who does everything for His people and finds sour fruit. The prophets mourn that the shepherds have destroyed the vineyard, and they promise a day when it will be fruitful and fill the world. Matthew 20 puts the owner back in the marketplace, calling people from outside into the work, and the whole movement of the Gospel is toward the nations coming in. The parable also anticipates the offence of Acts and Galatians, in which Gentile believers receive the Spirit without the burden of the law, and some who have borne it are angry.

The chapter sets up the cross with unusual directness. The third announcement is the clearest outline of the passion in the Gospel, and the ransom saying tells why the Son of Man goes. All that follows in Matthew, the entry into Jerusalem, the temple, the last supper, Gethsemane and Calvary, is the Son of Man giving His life for many, and the cup He drinks is the cup the prophets saw.

The story ends where the last verse of the chapter points. The blind men receive sight and follow Him, and in the new creation the redeemed see the face of the One who bought them, Revelation 22:4. The last will be first in a kingdom where the Lamb is the lamp, and every worker, early and late, receives the full wage that the owner's goodness provides, a place in the household of God and a share in the reign of the One who served.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the vineyard workers chiefly teach?

options.text: God gives the kingdom by free grace, not as wages earned, which offends the merit-minded heart.
options.note: The equal wage and the owner's freedom to be generous picture grace, exposing the grumblers.

options.text: That everyone should be paid the same regardless of hours worked.
options.note: It uses wages as an image, but its subject is God's grace, not labor policy.

options.text: That the first workers were treated unfairly by the landowner.
options.note: The owner insists he wronged no one; they received exactly what was agreed.

options.text: That God rewards strictly according to how much we do.
options.note: The parable teaches the opposite, that God gives freely, not by strict measure of work.

quiz.q: How does Jesus define greatness in His kingdom?

options.text: The one who wants to be great must be a servant, and the first must be a slave of all.
options.note: Verses 26-27 invert worldly greatness into service.

options.text: Great leaders should use their authority wisely over others.
options.note: That is closer to the Gentile pattern Jesus rejects; greatness is serving, not ruling well.

options.text: Greatness comes from securing the most honored positions.
options.note: That is exactly the request Jesus corrects; the seats are not the path to greatness.

options.text: Greatness is unimportant and should never be desired at all.
options.note: Jesus redirects the desire for greatness toward service rather than forbidding it outright.

quiz.q: Why did the Son of Man come, according to verse 28?

options.text: Not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
options.note: Verse 28 states the purpose of Jesus' death as a ransom.

options.text: To serve people by teaching and healing them.
options.note: He did serve in these ways, but the verse climaxes in giving His life as a ransom, which this omits.

options.text: To establish His right to be served as King.
options.note: The opposite; He came not to be served but to serve.

options.text: To show that self-sacrifice is unnecessary for greatness.
options.note: His self-sacrifice is the very definition and ground of greatness here.

quiz.q: What marks the two blind men outside Jericho?

options.text: They persist in crying to the Son of David for mercy, are healed, and follow Jesus.
options.note: Verses 30-34 show their persistent faith, healing, and discipleship.

options.text: They ask Jesus for money as beggars by the road.
options.note: They were beggars, but they asked for sight and mercy, not money.

options.text: They are silenced by the crowd and give up.
options.note: The crowd tried to silence them, but they cried out all the louder.

options.text: They are healed but then walk away from Jesus.
options.note: Having received sight, they followed Him.

questions: The all-day workers resented the owner's generosity to others. Where does grace shown to someone else stir envy or a sense of being owed in your heart?
God asks, are you envious because I am generous? How would gladness in His goodness to others change the way you view your own lot?
Jesus measures greatness by service. In your home, work, or church, where is He calling you to lead by serving rather than by being served?
The Son of Man gave His life as a ransom for you. How does dwelling on that price reshape your grip on status and your willingness to give?
The blind men cried out all the louder when told to be quiet. What need should you keep bringing to Jesus even when others would hush you?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts add For many are called, but few are chosen, as at Matthew 22:14; the saying that frames the parable is the last will be first, and the first will be last.
Some manuscripts add and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized, drawn from Mark 10:38-39; the cup Jesus speaks of is His coming suffering and death.
